items.stem: Briefly explain why the multi-stakeholder model is used for internet governance.
items.answer: The internet is run by many actors across borders – engineers, companies, governments, users – so decisions about domains and standards need technical expertise and broad legitimacy rather than control by one state.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The internet is run by many actors across borders – engineers, companies, governments, users – so decisions about domains and standards need technical expertise and broad legitimacy rather than control by one state. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between throttling and a full internet shutdown.
items.answer: A full shutdown cuts off internet access entirely in an area; throttling slows connections or specific services, making them nearly unusable while appearing to remain on.
items.markingKey: A full shutdown cuts off internet access entirely in an area; throttling slows connections or specific services, making them nearly unusable while appearing to remain on. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The government of a state with an annual GDP of US$40 billion orders a complete internet shutdown lasting 240 hours. Assume the digital economy contributes 3% of GDP and is entirely stopped by the shutdown. Estimate the economic cost in US$ millions.
items.answer: about US$32.9 million
items.markingKey: Digital economy per day = 40 bn × 3% ÷ 365 = US$3.3 m [M1]; × 240/24 days = US$32.9 m [M1 A1].

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Internet shutdowns only affect social media." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Shutdowns cut off banking, health information, emergency communication, education and businesses for everyone in the area.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Iran's National Information Network shows the splinternet.
items.answer: Iran has built a domestic network that allows local services to keep running while international access is cut, as during the November 2019 fuel-price protests. A national intranet lets the state cut off global communication with less economic damage, fragmenting the internet along borders.
items.markingKey: Context (Iran has built a domestic network that allows local services to keep running while international access is cut, as during the November 2019 fuel-price protests.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: "Internet shutdowns are never justified." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Shutdowns are almost never proportionate because they affect everyone; targeted, lawful measures against specific content are less harmful alternatives.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they violate free expression and access to information (UN Human Rights Council); large economic costs; evidence that they reduce violence is weak. Arguments against: governments argue short, local shutdowns can stop incitement during riots; some cite exam cheating or emergencies. items.stem: Explain why net neutrality matters for innovation and fairness.
items.answer: If ISPs could charge for priority or block services, large firms could pay for fast lanes while start-ups and non-profits were slowed, and ISPs could favour their own services, reducing competition and access to information.

items.markingKey: Mob lynchings. Rumours about child kidnappers led to deadly attacks.

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Nobody controls the internet." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: No single body controls it, but ICANN coordinates names and numbers, ISPs and states control access, standards bodies set protocols and large platforms control most traffic – power is distributed but real.
items.markingKey: No single body controls it, but ICANN coordinates names and numbers, ISPs and states control access, standards bodies set protocols and large platforms control most traffic – power is distributed but real. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between spear phishing and phishing.
items.answer: Phishing sends generic fraudulent messages to many people; spear phishing targets specific individuals with personalised messages using information about them.
items.markingKey: Phishing sends generic fraudulent messages to many people; spear phishing targets specific individuals with personalised messages using information about them. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Social media is the main cause of political polarisation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Polarisation began rising in some countries before social media, and is also driven by partisan media, economic inequality and party strategies; social media can amplify it.
items.markingKey: Polarisation began rising in some countries before social media, and is also driven by partisan media, economic inequality and party strategies; social media can amplify it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the multilateral (state-led) model and the multi-stakeholder model.
items.answer: The multi-stakeholder model includes companies, technical bodies and civil society alongside governments (e.g. ICANN); the multilateral model gives states the main decision-making role, as some governments propose through the UN's ITU.
items.markingKey: The multi-stakeholder model includes companies, technical bodies and civil society alongside governments (e.g. ICANN); the multilateral model gives states the main decision-making role, as some governments propose through the UN's ITU. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why humans are often described as the weakest link in cybersecurity.
items.answer: Attackers exploit trust, urgency and curiosity through phishing and social engineering; one person clicking a link or reusing a password can bypass technical defences.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Attackers exploit trust, urgency and curiosity through phishing and social engineering; one person clicking a link or reusing a password can bypass technical defences. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why personalisation algorithms can create filter bubbles.
items.answer: They rank content by predicted engagement based on past behaviour, so users see more of what they already like and less that challenges them, narrowing exposure over time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They rank content by predicted engagement based on past behaviour, so users see more of what they already like and less that challenges them, narrowing exposure over time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The government of a region with an annual GDP of US$450 billion orders a complete internet shutdown lasting 120 hours. Assume the digital economy contributes 3% of GDP and is entirely stopped by the shutdown. Estimate the economic cost in US$ millions.
items.answer: about US$184.9 million
items.markingKey: Digital economy per day = 450 bn × 3% ÷ 365 = US$37.0 m [M1]; × 120/24 days = US$184.9 m [M1 A1].

items.stem: A password has 12 characters chosen from lower-case letters only (26 possible characters). Calculate the number of possible passwords and the worst-case time to try them all at 10⁶ guesses per second.
items.markingKey: 26^12 = 9.54 × 10¹⁶ combinations [M1 A1]; ÷ 10⁶ = 9.54 × 10¹⁰ s ≈ 3,020 years [A1].

items.stem: Outline one way in which Facebook in Myanmar shows the social impact of networks.
items.answer: Facebook was the main gateway to the internet for many in Myanmar; hate speech against the Rohingya spread widely before and during the 2017 violence, and the UN fact-finding mission (2018) said Facebook played a "determining role". An engagement-driven platform with weak local-language moderation amplified hate in a fragile context, contributing to real-world violence.
items.markingKey: Context (Facebook was the main gateway to the internet for many in Myanmar; hate speech against the Rohingya spread widely before and during the 2017 violence, and the UN fact-finding mission (2018) said Facebook played a "determining role".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: an engagement-driven platform with weak local-language moderation amplified hate in a fragile context, contributing to real-world violence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the social impact of networks.

items.stem: Using Iran's National Information Network as an example, explain the splinternet.
items.answer: Iran has built a domestic network that allows local services to keep running while international access is cut, as during the November 2019 fuel-price protests. A national intranet lets the state cut off global communication with less economic damage, fragmenting the internet along borders.
items.markingKey: Context (Iran has built a domestic network that allows local services to keep running while international access is cut, as during the November 2019 fuel-price protests.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a national intranet lets the state cut off global communication with less economic damage, fragmenting the internet along borders. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the splinternet.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Amateurs hack systems; professionals hack people."
— Bruce Schneier, security technologist, 2000

Explain what the source suggests about cybersecurity.
items.answer: Skilled attackers target human behaviour (phishing, social engineering) because people are easier to manipulate than well-designed systems, so security must address people as well as technology.
items.markingKey: Skilled attackers target human behaviour (phishing, social engineering) because people are easier to manipulate than well-designed systems, so security must address people as well as technology. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A rumour is posted by 1 account on a group chat network. In each round of sharing, every person who has just received it passes it to 4 new people. Calculate how many people receive it in round 6, and the total number reached after 6 rounds (including the original poster).
items.answer: 4,096 in round 6; 5,461 in total

items.stem: The government of a country with an annual GDP of US$250 billion orders a complete internet shutdown lasting 240 hours. Assume the digital economy contributes 8% of GDP and is entirely stopped by the shutdown. Estimate the economic cost in US$ millions.
items.answer: about US$547.9 million
items.markingKey: Digital economy per day = 250 bn × 8% ÷ 365 = US$54.8 m [M1]; × 240/24 days = US$547.9 m [M1 A1].

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Organisations should never pay ransomware demands."
items.answer: As a policy, not paying reduces incentives for attackers, but there may be rare life-critical cases; prevention and backups are the real solution.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: payment funds criminal groups and encourages more attacks; no guarantee data will be restored; possible sanctions violations. Arguments against: hospitals may need to restore systems to save lives; paying may be cheaper than prolonged disruption; insurers sometimes cover payments. Supported judgement: As a policy, not paying reduces incentives for attackers, but there may be rare life-critical cases; prevention and backups are the real solution.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that social media algorithms are responsible for increasing polarisation in society.
items.answer: Algorithms can amplify division, especially for highly engaged users and in fragile contexts, but they are one contributor among several.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: engagement optimisation amplifies divisive content (Facebook Files); filter bubbles narrow exposure. Arguments against: research finds limited bubble effects for most users; polarisation predates social media in some countries (e.g. the US); partisan TV and offline networks matter. Supported judgement: Algorithms can amplify division, especially for highly engaged users and in fragile contexts, but they are one contributor among several. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that internet shutdowns are never justified.
items.answer: Shutdowns are almost never proportionate because they affect everyone; targeted, lawful measures against specific content are less harmful alternatives.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they violate free expression and access to information (UN Human Rights Council); large economic costs; evidence that they reduce violence is weak. Arguments against: governments argue short, local shutdowns can stop incitement during riots; some cite exam cheating or emergencies. Supported judgement: Shutdowns are almost never proportionate because they affect everyone; targeted, lawful measures against specific content are less harmful alternatives. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Cybersecurity is mainly the responsibility of individual users." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Users play a part, but responsibility lies mostly with organisations, vendors and governments that design and regulate systems.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: users choose passwords, click links and install updates; awareness training reduces phishing success. Arguments against: organisations and vendors design systems and set defaults; governments set standards (e.g. bans on default passwords); state-level attacks exceed individual capacity. Supported judgement: Users play a part, but responsibility lies mostly with organisations, vendors and governments that design and regulate systems. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.
